title: Runtime kernel integration experiments — Triton/TensorRT/custom kernels (draft notes)
content:
Context and goal:

This is a working note capturing the design/experiment space and early results when integrating TensorRT (TRT), NVIDIA Triton, and our custom fused-kernel prototypes into the Redwood serving runtime. Goal: identify practical tradeoffs (latency, throughput, memory, engineering complexity) and surface recommendations for a phased rollout strategy that preserves our runtime guarantees (latency SLOs, graceful degradation, KV cache correctness).

High-level summary (TL;DR):
- TensorRT yields the best per-GPU token throughput for FP16 and INT8 on decoder-only models when the end-to-end pipeline can be compiled into an optimized engine, but engineering & model support gaps are non-trivial.
- Triton simplifies deployment (model reps + model control API, batching) and provides maturity (model repository, metrics, autoscale hooks), but the default dynamic batching has observable tail latency variability under small-queue SLOs.
- Custom fused kernels (attention + rotary + layernorm fusion) give the largest p99 latency reduction in microbenchmarks for short-sequence, low-latency requests but are expensive to maintain and have portability limits across GPU generations and driver versions.
- KV cache integration is the trickiest cross-cutting concern: pinned host memory vs device-resident cache tradeoffs, stream synchronization, and cache eviction policies impact both latency and throughput.

Experiment matrix (we ran microbenchmarks on g5.12x with A10G-equivalent; model: 7B decoder-only; batch sizes: 1..8; seq_len: 8/32/128; tokens-per-request: 8):

Configurations tested:
- Baseline: PyTorch+FasterTransformer-like custom runtime with continuous batching (existing serving runtime).
- TRT-full: Export-to-ONNX -> TensorRT engine (FP16), single TRT engine per model/version.
- TRT-int8: TRT with calibration table (per-model), INT8 performance test (only supported for model variants we can calibrate deterministically).
- Triton-backend: Triton GRPC + http, using tritonserver with TensorRT backend for compiled engines and torchscript for fallback.
- Custom-fused: Our prototype fused attention kernels (CUDA 11.8, custom kernels compiled with nvcc) integrated into runtime via a plugin layer.

Micro results (representative):
- Throughput (tokens/s, single GPU, seq_len=32, batch=4):
  - Baseline: 42k tokens/s
  - TRT-FP16: 62k tokens/s (+48%)
  - TRT-INT8: 78k tokens/s (+86%) where calibration worked
  - Triton(TensorRT backend): 59k tokens/s (overhead of model server ~5%)
  - Custom-fused: 70k tokens/s (+67%) but at higher GPU memory usage

- P99 latency (ms, seq_len=8, batch=1):
  - Baseline: 18 ms
  - TRT-FP16: 22 ms (higher due to engine warmup / kernel launch coalescing when batch=1)
  - TRT-INT8: 24 ms
  - Triton: 30 ms (server overhead + batching heuristic delays)
  - Custom-fused: 12 ms (best for single-token low-latency requests)
Observations on numbers: these are microbenchmarks — real-world tail depends heavily on arrival patterns and KV cache hit rates. TRT shines for throughput at moderate batch sizes; our fused kernel shines for extremely low-latency single-request SLOs. Triton is close to TRT in throughput but has p99 variability due to its dynamic batching window.

Detailed tradeoffs:

1) Performance vs latency SLOs:
- TRT engines optimize for throughput; for batch=1 latency-sensitive workloads we observed worse p50/p99 due to kernel launch batching and engine optimizations expecting larger parallelism.
- Custom fused kernels reduce per-token overhead (fewer kernel launches, combined memory accesses), unlocking lower p99 for tiny sequences.

2) Engineering and ops complexity:
- Triton: low ops friction for deployment lifecycle (model repository, model-control API, model metrics), easier to canary and swap models, integrates with GPU managers.
- TRT: requires export pipeline (onnx) and careful handling of ops not supported by TRT—fallback paths increase complexity. INT8 requires a per-model calibration pipeline and adds versioning complexity.
- Custom kernels: large engineering cost (testing across CUDA versions, GPU archs, correctness/precision checks), slower rollout.

3) Portability and maintenance:
- Triton and TRT-backed deployments are portable across clusters with NVIDIA GPUs, but TRT engines are often tightly coupled to driver/CUDA versions and GPU compute capability; recompile/re-export needed for major infra changes.
- Custom kernels have the worst portability (arch-specific optimizations) and require long-term maintenance budgets.

4) KV cache integration specifics:
- Options: device-resident KV cache (GPU memory), host-pinned cache (page-locked host memory tunneled to device), or hybrid (LRU-like host backing).
- Device-resident cache gives lowest lookup latency but high memory footprint—limits max concurrent sessions per GPU.
- Host-pinned reduces GPU memory pressure but incurs PCIe/NVLink copy latency. For small seqs, the copy overhead dominates and hurts p99.
- Triton + TRT: Triton’s memory manager and model control make lifecycle easier, but ensuring cache lifetime across model reloads is non-trivial (need hooks to flush/persist cache during model swap).
- Custom kernels allowed us to colocate KV indexes and attention kernels to avoid copies, resulting in 10–20% lower p99 for short sequences in tests, but required non-trivial runtime changes (new allocator, per-request stream affinity).

5) Scheduling and batching policy effects:
- Continuous batching (our current runtime heuristic) packs incoming requests aggressively; great for throughput but causes queueing delays for tight SLOs when queue depth spikes.
- Fixed-window batching (Triton-style) offers predictable latency windows but can waste cycles at low QPS.
- Hybrid policy idea: latency-first routing for tokens<=12 and batch<=1 requests -> route to custom-fused engine or GPU pool pinned to low-latency mode; throughput-first routing for long generations -> route to TRT engines optimized for batch size >=4. Early experiments with a two-pool policy reduced p99 by ~30% for mixed workloads while preserving aggregate throughput.

Operational risks and mitigations:
- Engine drift: TRT engines built against library X may behave differently with driver Y. Mitigation: create CI matrix that auto-builds & smoke-tests TRT engines against supported driver versions and pins supported combinations in release notes.
- Calibration regressions (INT8): automated calibration validation harness with holdout prompts and a small eval set to detect quality regressions before rollout.
- Cache corruption during model swap: require atomic handoff protocols and safe draining/flush operations in model-controller paths.

Decision matrix (recommended):
- Short-term (0–3 months): adopt Triton for model lifecycle + TRT backend for production throughput workloads where (a) models export cleanly to ONNX/TRT and (b) latency SLOs are moderate. Keep baseline runtime for low-latency critical routes.
- Medium-term (3–9 months): harden custom-fused kernels as an opt-in low-latency path. Build a packaged abstraction (kernel-plugin API + CI) to reduce maintenance surface. Implement two-pool routing (low-latency pool + high-throughput pool) and autoscaling policies per pool.
- Long-term (9–18 months): invest in operator tooling to automate TRT engine builds (per-driver), INT8 calibration pipelines, and integrate KV cache lifecycle hooks with model-control so engines and cache snapshots can be atomically swapped. Assess if more of the fused-kernel logic can be upstreamed into an OSS kernel library to reduce maintenance burden.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Can we reduce TRT p99 for batch=1 by pre-warming engines or using CUDA graphs at request time? Quick experiment planned: record CUDA-graph replay for recurring prompt prefixes and measure p99 impact.
- Quantization safety: how broad is our model set where INT8 is safe? Need a broader eval across more models + downstream eval metrics.
- Cache eviction policy: design hybrid host/GPU KV cache with LRU-ish policy that is latency-aware — simulate with traces from production traffic (task: Ethan to provide representative traces).
- Kernel portability: test custom-fused build on Ampere vs Ada-generation GPUs; measure performance delta and compilation issues.

Action items (owners):
- Ethan: collect 2 weeks of production arrival traces + request size distribution (due 2025-02-02).
- Marina: prototype two-pool routing changes in the runtime (branch: routing/two-pool) and run mixed-workload sims (due 2025-02-20).
- Dmitri: CI for TRT engine build matrix and smoke tests (PR referenced in linked_artifacts) (start 2025-01-15).
- Sofia: prototype host-pinned KV cache path and microbench copy latencies across NVLink/PCIe (due 2025-02-10).

Notes / miscellaneous:
- We should tag the Triton experiments with explicit model-version artifacts to make rollbacks straightforward.
- Keep user-visible metrics: per-route p50/p90/p99, tokens/s, cache hit-rate, engine-version. Expose in Console.

Appendix: quick checklist for any TRT/Triton rollout
- Validate ONNX export parity for model ops (unit tests).
- Create calibration/eval harness if INT8 is used.
- Capture TensorRT engine build configs in infra-as-code (dockerfiles + build scripts).
- Add model-control hooks to gracefully pause traffic, snapshot KV cache, swap engine, and resume.

End of draft.

(Comments welcome — this is intentionally conversational and incomplete; will iterate once we have traces and initial two-pool sim results.)
